lines.text: The storeroom door closes for the last time. This time, the key turns in the hand of the law.
Silas Venn did not die of a tired heart. He died because he did the honest thing — and told the wrong man he was going to do it.
Somewhere in the market, a stallholder finds a small black envelope sealed with a silver anchor. It was never delivered. It was never meant to be.
The night market closes at midnight. The lanterns go out one by one, and the smell of rain on hot stone hangs over the stalls.
Silas Venn locks his storeroom from the inside, the way he always does when he stays late with the accounts. He pours his evening tea. He opens the ledger.
By morning the tea is cold, the ledger is torn, and Silas Venn is dead. The door is still locked. Nobody ever asked who held the other key.

solve.solutionHTML:
The Bookseller's Last Chapter — Solved

Henri Delacroix had been skimming the market association's funds for years, inventing rare-book sales and pocketing the money. Silas Venn found the phantom entries, drafted an audit letter — and, trusting his friend, told Henri about it on the phone the night before he died.

Henri bought foxglove tincture at Maison Herbal, signing 'H.D.', and asked how much would stop a heart. He knew Silas's tea blend. That night he slipped the tincture into Silas's evening tea, waited, and locked the storeroom from outside with the duplicate key he had cut three weeks earlier — staging a locked room and a heart attack.

No single clue convicts him. The ledger proves the theft, the logbook proves the poison, and the key receipt proves the access. Together, they leave no one else standing.

twists.body: The apothecary's cleaned-up tape changes everything: the foxglove buyer didn't just buy poison — he asked, in plain words, how much of it would stop a heart. But the tape is old, the voice is muffled, and the herbalist admits she has sold foxglove to gardeners for years. Was the buyer a murderer — or a gardener who asked a careless question? And if Henri bought the poison, why did he sign his own initials?
twists.title: The Buyer Asked How Much Would Stop a Heart

twists.body: Confronted, Henri breaks — but not the way you expect. He swears he only meant to make Silas sleep through the audit meeting, that he misjudged the dose, that he never meant to kill his friend. The ledger says theft. The poison says intent. The man in front of you says accident. The board, not his tears, decides which story is true.
twists.title: He Only Meant to Make Him Sleep
